title: Headache
practice_hpi: {{patient_name}} is a woman in her late twenties who presents with worsening daily headaches over several weeks. The headaches are worse in the morning and when she bears down or strains. She describes brief episodes where her vision goes dark for a few seconds, a whooshing sound in her ears that pulses with her heartbeat, and occasional double vision when she looks to the side. She has gained about 30 pounds over the past year. She denies recent head trauma, fever, neck stiffness, weakness, or numbness. She is not pregnant. She takes oral contraceptives.
hpi: {{patient_name}} presents with chronic daily headache (worse in morning, with Valsalva), transient visual obscurations, pulsatile tinnitus, and diplopia (CN VI palsy from increased ICP). Fundoscopy: bilateral papilledema. IIH is elevated ICP without mass lesion or hydrocephalus, typically in obese women of childbearing age. Risk factors: obesity, recent weight gain, vitamin A excess, tetracyclines, OCPs, steroids. Diagnosis: MRI/MRV brain (normal — rules out mass, venous sinus thrombosis). LP: elevated opening pressure (>25 cm H2O) with normal CSF composition. Treatment: weight loss (most important), acetazolamide (carbonic anhydrase inhibitor — reduces CSF production). Serial ophthalmology: visual fields, optic nerve exam. If vision threatened: optic nerve sheath fenestration or CSF shunting (VP or LP shunt). Discontinue causative medications.
